writing.prompt: Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay on the saying “What is worth doing is worth doing well ”, You should write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words.
writing.sample: The proverb "What is worth doing is worth doing well" carries a simple yet profound message: once we decide that something is worth our effort, we should pursue excellence rather than settle for a careless, half-finished job. I firmly agree with this view.To begin with, doing things well is the surest path to personal growth. When a student is devoted to a task and strives for perfection, every detail he polishes sharpens his own ability. Take my roommate, who rewrote his graduation thesis five times; the effort not only earned him an honour but also trained the patience he now relies on at work.Furthermore, the spirit of doing well drives society forward. Great engineers and craftsmen who spare no effort to refine their products give us the reliable bridges, phones and medicines we depend on every day. Had they been content with a rough result, progress would slow and quality would collapse.In conclusion, whatever is worth our time deserves our very best. As young students, we should abandon the get-it-done-quickly attitude and devote ourselves to every task, big or small, until it is truly done well.

transcript.en: M: You are a professor of physics at the University of Oxford. You're a senior advisor at the European Organization for Nuclear Research. You also seem to tour the globe tirelessly, giving talks. And in addition, you have your own weekly TV show on science. Where do you get the energy?
transcript.zh: M: 您是牛津大学的物理学教授，也是欧洲核子研究组织的高级顾问。您似乎还在不停地周游世界，发表演讲。此外，您还有自己的每周科学电视节目。您哪儿来的这么多精力？

transcript.en: W: Oh, well, I just love what I do. I'm extremely fortunate to have this life, doing what I love doing.
transcript.zh: W: 哦，是这样，我就是热爱自己所做的事情。我非常幸运，能够过着这样的生活，做自己喜欢做的事。

transcript.en: M: Professor, what exactly is your goal? Why do you do all of these?
transcript.zh: M: 教授，您的目标究竟是什么？您为什么要做这一切？

transcript.en: W: Well, as you said, I do have different things going on. But these, I think, can be divided into two groups: the education of science and the further understanding of science.
transcript.zh: W: 嗯，正如您所说，我确实同时在做不同的事情。但我认为，这些事情可以分为两类：科学教育和进一步理解科学。

transcript.en: M: Don't these two things get in the way of each other? What I mean is, doesn't giving lectures take time away from the lab?
transcript.zh: M: 这两件事不会互相妨碍吗？我的意思是，发表演讲不会占用您在实验室里的时间吗？

transcript.en: W: Not really, no. I love teaching, and I don't mind spending more time doing that now than in the past. Also, what I will say is that teaching a subject helps me comprehend it better myself. I find that it furthers my own knowledge when I have to explain something clearly, when I have to aid others in understanding it, and when I have to answer questions about it. Teaching at a high level can be very stimulating for anyone, no matter how much expertise they may already have in the field they are instructing.
transcript.zh: W: 不会，确实不会。我喜欢教学，而且现在比过去多花些时间做这件事，我也不介意。另外，我想说的是，教授一门学科有助于我自己更好地理解它。当我必须清楚地解释某件事、帮助别人理解它，以及回答有关它的问题时，我发现自己的知识也会因此得到拓展。无论一个人在所教授的领域中已经有多么丰富的专业知识，高水平的教学都能对他产生很大的启发。

transcript.en: M: Are there any scientific breakthroughs that you see on the near horizon, a significant discovery or invention we can expect soon?
transcript.zh: M: 您认为近期会出现什么科学突破吗？比如我们很快就能期待的重大​​发现或发明？

transcript.en: W: The world is always conducting science, and there are constantly new things being discovered. In fact, right now we have too much data sitting in computers. For example, we have thousands of photos of planet Mars taken by telescopes that nobody has ever seen. We have them, yet nobody has had time to look at them with their own eyes, let alone analyze them.
transcript.zh: W: 世界各地一直都在进行科学研究，不断有新事物被发现。事实上，我们现在有太多数据堆积在电脑里了。比如，望远镜拍摄了数千张火星的照片，却从来没有人看过。照片是有的，但还没有人有时间亲眼查看，更不用说分析它们了。

In the past, during the times of ancient Egypt, Greece or China, people used to believe that dreams could foresee the future. But today, with all the scientific knowledge that we have, I think it's much harder to believe in these sorts of things.

transcript.en: W: My grandmother is superstitious, and she thinks dreams can predict the future. Once she dreamed that the flight she was due to take the following day crashed. Can you guess what she did? She didn't take that flight. She didn't even bother to go to the airport the following day. Instead, she took the same flight but a week later. And everything was fine, of course. No plane ever crashed.
transcript.zh: W: 我祖母很迷信，她认为梦可以预示未来。有一次，她梦见自己第二天要乘坐的航班坠毁了。你猜她做了什么？她没有乘坐那趟航班，甚至第二天都懒得去机场。相反，她乘坐了同一航班，不过是在一周之后。当然，一切都很顺利。根本没有飞机坠毁。

transcript.en: M: How funny! Did you know that flying is actually safer than any other mode of transport? It's been statistically proven. People can be so irrational sometimes.
transcript.zh: M: 真有意思！你知道乘飞机其实比其他任何交通方式都安全吗？这在统计数据上已经得到了证明。人有时候真的会很不理性。

transcript.en: W: Yes, absolutely. But even if we think they are ridiculous, emotions can be just as powerful as rational thinking.
transcript.zh: W: 是的，完全正确。不过，即使我们觉得这些想法很荒谬，情感也可以和理性思维一样强大。

transcript.en: M: Exactly. People do all sorts of crazy things because of their irrational feelings. But in fact, some psychologists believe that our dreams are the result of our emotions and memories from that day. I think it was Sigmund Freud who said that children's dreams were usually simple representations of their wishes, things they wished would happen. But in adults, dreams are much more complicated reflections of their more sophisticated sentiments.
transcript.zh: M: 没错。人们会因为不理性的情感而做出各种疯狂的事情。但事实上，一些心理学家认为，我们的梦是那一天的情感和记忆所产生的结果。我记得是西格蒙德·弗洛伊德说过，儿童的梦通常是他们愿望的简单呈现，也就是他们希望发生的事情。但对成年人来说，梦则是他们更复杂、更成熟的情感的复杂反映。

transcript.en: W: Isn't it interesting how psychologists try to understand using the scientific method something as bizarre as dreams? Psychology is like the rational study of irrational feelings.
transcript.zh: W: 心理学家试图用科学方法去理解像梦这样奇怪的事物，难道不是很有意思吗？心理学就像是对非理性情感进行的理性研究。

transcript.en: While some scientists explore the surface of Antarctica, others are learning more about a giant body of water four kilometers beneath the ice pack. Scientists first discovered Lake Vostok in the 1970s by using radio waves that penetrate the ice. Since then, they have used sound waves and even satellites to map this massive body of water.
transcript.zh: 一些科学家在探索南极洲的地表，另一些科学家则在进一步了解冰盖下方四千米处的一片巨大水体。20世纪70年代，科学家首次利用能够穿透冰层的无线电波发现了沃斯托克湖。此后，他们又利用声波，甚至卫星，对这片巨大的水体进行了测绘。

transcript.en: How does the water in Lake Vostok remain liquid beneath an ice sheet? "The thick glacier above acts like an insulating blanket and keeps the water from freezing," says Martin Siegert, a glaciologist from the University of Wales. In addition, geothermal heat from deep within the earth may warm the hidden lake. The scientists suspect that micro-organisms may be living in Lake Vostok, closed off from the outside world for more than 2 million years.
transcript.zh: 沃斯托克湖的水为何能在冰盖下保持液态？“上方厚厚的冰川就像一条隔热毯，防止湖水结冰，”威尔士大学的冰川学家马丁·西格特说。此外，来自地球深处的地热也可能使这个隐秘的湖泊保持温暖。科学家怀疑，沃斯托克湖中可能存在微生物，而这个湖泊已与外界隔绝了超过200万年。

transcript.en: Anything found there will be totally alien to what's on the surface of the earth, says Siegert. Scientists are trying to find a way to drill into the ice and draw water samples without causing contamination. Again, robots might be the solution. If all goes as planned, a drill-shaped robot will melt through the surface ice. When it reaches the lake, it will release another robot that can swim in the lake, take pictures, and look for signs of life.
transcript.zh: 西格特说，在那里发现的任何东西都将与地球表面的事物完全不同。科学家正在设法钻入冰层并抽取水样，同时避免造成污染。机器人或许又能成为解决方案。如果一切按计划进行，一台钻头形状的机器人将融穿表层冰层。当它抵达湖泊时，会释放出另一台能够在湖中游动、拍摄照片并寻找生命迹象的机器人。

transcript.en: The scientists hope their discoveries will shed light on life in outer space, which might exist in similar dark and airless conditions. Recently, close-up pictures of Jupiter's moon, Europa, show signs of water beneath its icy surface. Once tested in Antarctica, robots could be sent to Europa to search for life there too.
transcript.zh: 科学家希望他们的发现能够为外太空的生命提供线索，因为那里可能存在处于类似黑暗且无空气环境中的生命。最近，木星的卫星 Europa 的特写照片显示，其冰封表面下方可能有水。机器人一旦在南极洲完成测试，就可以被派往 Europa，在那里寻找生命。

transcript.en: The idea to study the American Indian tribe Tarahumaras came to James Copeland in 1984 when he discovered that very little research had been done on their language. He contacted a tribe member through a social worker who worked with the tribesmen in Mexico. At first, the tribe member, named Gonzalez, was very reluctant to cooperate. He told Copeland that no amount of money could buy his language. But after Copeland explained to him what he intended to do with his research and how it would benefit the Tarahumaras, Gonzalez agreed to help. He took Copeland to his village and served as an intermediary. Copeland says, "Thanks to him, the Tarahumaras understood what our mission was and started trusting us."
transcript.zh: 1984年，詹姆斯·科普兰发现关于美国印第安部落塔拉乌马拉人的语言几乎没有开展过研究，于是产生了研究这个部落的想法。他通过一名在墨西哥与部落成员一起工作的社会工作者联系上了一位部落成员。起初，这位名叫冈萨雷斯的部落成员非常不愿意合作。他告诉科普兰，再多的钱也买不到他的语言。但在科普兰向他解释了自己打算如何开展研究，以及这项研究将如何使塔拉乌马拉人受益之后，冈萨雷斯同意提供帮助。他带科普兰去了自己的村庄，并担任中间人。科普兰说：“多亏了他，塔拉乌马拉人才明白我们的使命是什么，并开始信任我们。”

transcript.en: Entering the world of the Tarahumaras has been a laborious project for Copeland. To reach their homeland he must drive two and a half days from Houston, Texas. He loads up his vehicle with goods that the tribesmen can't easily get, and gives the goods to them as a gesture of friendship. The Tarahumaras, who don't believe in accumulating wealth, take the food and share it among themselves.
transcript.zh: 对科普兰来说，进入塔拉乌马拉人的世界是一个艰苦的项目。为了到达他们的家园，他必须从得克萨斯州休斯敦驾车两天半。他把部落成员不容易获得的物资装满车辆，并将这些物资送给他们，以示友好。塔拉乌马拉人不相信积累财富，他们收下食物，并在彼此之间分享。

transcript.en: For Copeland, the experience has not only been academically satisfying, but also has enriched his life in several ways. "I see people rejecting technology and living a very hard, traditional life, which offers me another notion about the meaning of progress in the western tradition," he says. "I experience the simplicity of living in nature that I would otherwise only be able to read about. I see a lot of beauty in their sense of sharing and concern for each other."
transcript.zh: 对科普兰来说，这段经历不仅在学术上令人满足，也在多个方面丰富了他的生活。他说：“我看到人们拒绝技术，过着非常艰苦的传统生活，这让我对西方传统中进步的含义有了另一种认识。我体验到了融入自然的简朴生活，否则我只能通过阅读来了解这种生活。我从他们分享和彼此关怀的观念中看到了许多美好。”

transcript.en: What is a radical? It seems today that people are terrified of the term, particularly of having the label attached to them. Accusing individuals or groups of being radical often serves to silence them into submission, thereby maintaining the existing state of affairs, and, more important, preserving the power of a select minority who are mostly wealthy white males in western society.
transcript.zh: 什么是激进派？如今，人们似乎对“激进”这个词感到恐惧，尤其害怕被贴上这样的标签。指责个人或群体激进，往往是为了迫使他们沉默并顺从，从而维护现状，更重要的是，维护西方社会中一个少数群体的权力，而这个群体主要由富有的白人男性组成。

transcript.en: Feminism is a perfect example of this phenomenon. The women's movement has been plagued by stereotypes, misrepresentations by the media, and accusations of man-hating and radicalism, when the basic foundation of feminism is simply that women deserve equal rights in all facets of life. When faced with the threat of being labelled radical, women back down from their worthy calls and consequently participate in their own oppression.
transcript.zh: 女权主义就是这一现象的一个典型例子。妇女运动一直饱受刻板印象、媒体的歪曲报道以及仇视男性和激进主义等指责的困扰，而女权主义的基本立场其实很简单：女性在生活的各个方面都应享有平等权利。当面临被贴上激进标签的威胁时，女性会放弃自己正当的诉求，因而参与到对自身的压迫之中。

transcript.en: It has gotten to the point that many women are afraid to call themselves feminists because of the stigma attached to the word. If people refuse to be controlled and intimidated by stigmas, the stigmas lose all their power. Without fear on which they feed, such stigmas can only die.
transcript.zh: 事情已经发展到这样的地步：许多女性因为“女权主义者”一词所带的污名，而不敢称自己为女权主义者。如果人们拒绝受污名的控制和恐吓，污名就会失去全部力量。没有恐惧作为滋养，这样的污名只能消亡。

transcript.en: To me, a radical is simply someone who rebels against the norm or advocates a change in the existing state of affairs. On close inspection, it becomes clear that the norm is constantly evolving and therefore is not a constant entity.
transcript.zh: 在我看来，激进派不过是反抗常规或主张改变现状的人。仔细考察便会发现，常规一直在不断演变，因此并不是一个恒定不变的事物。

transcript.en: So why then is deviation from the present situation such a threat when the state of affairs itself is unstable and subject to relentless transformation?
transcript.zh: 那么，既然现状本身不稳定且不断发生变化，偏离当前状况为何会构成如此大的威胁呢？

transcript.en: It all goes back to maintaining the power of those who have it and preventing the right of those who don't. In fact, when we look at the word "radical" in a historical context, nearly every figure we now hold up as a hero was considered a radical in his or her time. Radicals are people who effect change. They are the people about whom history is written. Abolitionists were radicals; civil rights activists were radicals; even the founders of our country in their fight to win independence from England were radicals. Their presence in history has changed the way our society functions, mainly by shifting the balance of power that previously existed. Of course, there are some radicals who've made a negative impact on humanity, but undeniably, there would simply be no progress without radicals. That being said, next time someone calls me a radical, I will accept that label with pride.
transcript.zh: 这一切都归结于维护掌权者的权力，以及阻止无权者获得权利。事实上，当我们从历史背景来看“激进”一词时，几乎每一位如今被我们视为英雄的人物，在其所处的时代都曾被认为是激进派。激进派是推动变革的人。他们是历史书写其事迹的人。废奴主义者是激进派；民权活动家是激进派；甚至我们国家的创建者们在争取脱离英国、赢得独立的斗争中也是激进派。他们在历史上的存在改变了我们社会的运行方式，主要是改变了原有的权力平衡。当然，也有一些激进派对人类产生了负面影响，但不可否认，如果没有激进派，就根本不会有进步。话虽如此，下一次有人称我为激进派时，我会自豪地接受这个标签。

transcript.en: We are very susceptible to the influence of the people around us. For instance, you may have known somebody who has gone overseas for a year or so and has returned with an accent, perhaps. We become part of our immediate environment. None of us are immune to the influences of our own world, and let us not kid ourselves that we are untouched by the things and the people in our life.
transcript.zh: 我们非常容易受到周围人的影响。例如，你可能认识这样一个人：他出国待了一年左右，回来时或许已经带上了口音。我们会成为身边环境的一部分。没有人能够不受自己所处世界的影响，所以不要自欺欺人，以为我们不会受到生活中的事物和人的影响。

transcript.en: Fred goes off to his new job at a factory. Fred takes his 10-minute coffee break, but the other workers take half an hour. Fred says, "What's the matter with you guys?" Two weeks later, Fred is taking 20-minute breaks. A month later, Fred takes his half hour. Fred is saying, "If you can't beat them, join them. Why should I work any harder than the next guy?"
transcript.zh: 弗雷德去一家工厂开始了新工作。弗雷德休息十分钟喝咖啡，但其他工人却休息半个小时。弗雷德说：“你们这是怎么回事？”两周后，弗雷德开始休息二十分钟。一个月后，弗雷德也休息半个小时。弗雷德说：“既然无法击败他们，那就加入他们。凭什么我要比别人更卖力地工作？”

transcript.en: The fascinating thing about being human is that generally we are unaware that there are changes taking place in our mentality. It is like returning to the city smog after some weeks in the fresh air—only then do we realize that we have become accustomed to the nasty smells. Mix with critical people and we learn to criticize; mix with happy people and we learn about happiness.
transcript.zh: 人类最令人着迷的一点在于，通常我们并没有意识到自己的心态正在发生变化。这就像在新鲜空气中待了几个星期后重新回到城市的烟雾中，只有在那时我们才会意识到，自己已经习惯了那些难闻的气味。和爱挑剔的人相处，我们就会学会批评；和快乐的人相处，我们就会学会了解幸福。

transcript.en: What this means is that we need to decide what we want from life and then choose our company accordingly. You may well say, "That is going to take some effort. It may not be comfortable. I may offend some of my present company." Right, but it is your life.
transcript.zh: 这意味着，我们需要决定自己想从生活中得到什么，然后据此选择与自己相伴的人。你很可能会说：“那需要付出一些努力。这样做可能会让人感到不自在。我可能会得罪现在身边的一些人。”没错，但这是你的人生。

transcript.en: Fred may say, "I'm always broke, frequently depressed. I'm going nowhere and I never do anything exciting." Then we discover that Fred's best friends are always broke, frequently depressed, going nowhere and wishing that life was more exciting. This is not a coincidence. Nor is it our business to stand in judgment of Fred. However, if Fred ever wants to improve his quality of life, the first thing he'll need to do is recognize what has been going on all these years.
transcript.zh: 弗雷德可能会说：“我总是身无分文，经常感到沮丧。我一事无成，也从来没有做过什么令人兴奋的事。”然后我们发现，弗雷德最要好的朋友也总是身无分文，经常感到沮丧，一事无成，并且总希望生活能更加精彩。这并非巧合。我们也没有资格对弗雷德妄加评判。然而，如果弗雷德有一天想要改善自己的生活质量，他首先需要做的，就是认识到这些年来一直发生着什么。

transcript.en: It's no surprise that doctors as a profession suffer a lot of ill health because they spend their lives around sick people. Psychiatrists have a higher incidence of suicide in their profession for related reasons. Traditionally, 9 out of 10 children whose parents smoke, smoke themselves. Obesity is in part an environmental problem. Successful people have successful friends. And so the story goes on.
transcript.zh: 医生这个职业的人健康状况普遍较差，并不令人意外，因为他们一生都在与病人相处。精神科医生的职业自杀率更高，原因与此相关。传统上，父母吸烟的孩子中，十个有九个也会吸烟。肥胖在一定程度上是一个环境问题。成功人士身边也都是成功人士。这样的例子还有很多。

transcript.en: Virtually every American can recognize a dollar bill at a mere glance. Many can identify it by its sound or texture. But few people indeed can accurately describe the world's most powerful, important currency.
transcript.zh: 几乎每个美国人只需一眼就能认出一张美元钞票。许多人甚至能凭声音或质感辨认出它。然而，真正能够准确描述这种世界上最强大、最重要的货币的人确实寥寥无几。

transcript.en: The American dollar bill is colored with black ink on one side and green on the other; the exact composition of the paper and ink is a closely guarded government secret. Despite its weighty importance, the dollar bill actually weighs little. It requires nearly 500 bills to tip the scales at a pound. Not only is the dollar bill lightweight, but it also has a brief life span. Few dollar bills survive longer than 18 months.
transcript.zh: 美元钞票一面用黑色油墨印刷，另一面用绿色油墨印刷；纸张和油墨的确切成分是政府严密保守的秘密。尽管美元钞票意义重大，但它实际上很轻。将近500张钞票才有一磅重。美元钞票不仅重量轻，而且使用寿命也很短。很少有美元钞票能保存超过18个月。

transcript.en: The word "dollar" is taken from the German word "thaler," the name for the world's most important currency in the 16th century. The thaler was a silver coin first minted in 1518 under the reign of Charles V, Emperor of Germany.
transcript.zh: “dollar”一词源自德语单词“thaler”，后者是16世纪世界上最重要的货币的名称。塔勒是一种银币，于1518年在德国皇帝查理五世统治时期首次铸造。

transcript.en: The concept of paper money is a relatively recent innovation in the history of American currency. When the Constitution was signed, people had little regard for paper money because of its steadily decreasing value during the colonial era. Because of this lack of faith, the new American government minted only coins for common currency. Interest-bearing bank notes were issued at the same time, but their purpose was limited to providing money for urgent government crises, such as American involvement in the War of 1812.
transcript.zh: 纸币的概念在美国货币史上是一项相对较新的创新。宪法签署时，人们对纸币并不看重，因为纸币在殖民时期的价值一直在下降。由于缺乏信任，新成立的美国政府只铸造硬币作为通用货币。与此同时，政府也发行了计息的银行券，但其用途仅限于为紧急的政府危机提供资金，例如美国参与1812年战争。

transcript.en: The first noninterest-bearing paper currency was authorized by Congress in 1862, at the height of the Civil War. At this point, citizens' old fears of devalued paper currency had calmed, and the dollar bill was born. The new green colored paper money quickly earned the nickname "greenback."
transcript.zh: 1862年内战最激烈的时期，国会批准发行了第一种不计息的纸币。此时，公民对于纸币贬值的旧有担忧已经平息，美元钞票由此诞生。这种新发行的绿色纸币很快获得了“绿背钞”的绰号。

transcript.en: Today, the American dollar bill is a product of the Federal Reserve, and is issued from the twelve Federal Reserve banks around the United States. The government keeps a steady supply of approximately two billion bills in circulation at all times.
transcript.zh: 如今，美元钞票由联邦储备系统发行，并由遍布美国的12家联邦储备银行发行。政府始终维持着大约20亿张钞票的流通量。

transcript.en: Controversy continues to surround the true value of the dollar bill. American history has seen generations of politicians argue in favor of a gold standard for American currency. However, for the present, the American dollar bill holds the value that is printed on it, and little more. The only other guarantee on the bill is a Federal Reserve pledge as a confirmation in the form of government securities.
transcript.zh: 关于美元钞票实际价值的争议一直存在。美国历史上，一代又一代的政治家都曾主张美国货币实行金本位制。然而，就目前而言，美元钞票的价值就是印在上面的面值，仅此而已。钞票上的唯一其他保障，是联邦储备系统以政府证券形式作出的保证，作为确认。

paragraphs.t: After years of big promises, telemedicine is finally living up to its potential. Driven by faster internet connections, ubiquitous(无处不在的) smartphones and changing insurance standards, more health providers are turning to electronic communications to do their jobs—and it's dramatically changing the delivery of healthcare.

Doctors are linking up with patients by phone, email and webcam(网络摄像头). They're also consulting with each other electronically—sometimes to make split-second decisions on heart attacks and strokes. Patients, meanwhile, are using new devices to relay their blood pressure, heart rate and other vital signs to their doctors so they can manage chronic conditions at home. Telemedicine also allows for better care in places where medical expertise is hard to come by. Five to 10 times a day, Doctors Without Borders relays questions about tough cases from its physicians in Niger, South Sudan and elsewhere to its network of 280 experts around the world, and back again via internet.

As a measure of how rapidly telemedicine is spreading, consider: More than 15 million Americans received some kind of medical care remotely last year, according to the American Telemedicine Association, a trade group, which expects those numbers to grow by 30% this year.

None of this is to say that telemedicine has found its way into all corners of medicine. A recent survey of 500 tech-savvy(精通技术的) consumers found that 39% hadn't heard of telemedicine, and of those who haven't used it, 42% said they preferred in-person doctor visits. In a poll of 1500 family physicians, only 15% had used it in their practices—but 90% said they would if it were appropriately reimbursed(补偿).

What's more, for all the rapid growth, significant questions and challenges remain. Rules defining and regulating telemedicine differ widely from state to state. Physicians groups are issuing different guidelines about what care they consider appropriate to deliver and in what form.

Some critics also question whether the quality of care is keeping up with the rapid expansion of telemedicine. And there's the question of what services physicians should be paid for: Insurance coverage varies from health plan to health plan, and a big federal plan covers only a narrow range of services. Telemedicine's future will depend on how—and whether—regulators, providers, payers and patients can address these challenges. Here's a closer look at some of these issues:

Do patients trade quality for convenience? The fastest-growing services in telemedicine connect consumers with clinicians they've never met for a phone, video or email visit—on-demand, 24/7. Typically, these are for nonemergency issues such as colds, flu, ear-aches and skin rashes, and they cost around $45, compared with approximately $100 at a doctor's office, $160 at an urgent-care clinic or $750 and up at an emergency room.

Many health plans and employers have rushed to offer the services and promote them as a convenient way for plan members to get medical care without leaving home or work. Nearly three-quarters of large employers will offer virtual doctor visits as a benefit to employees this year, up from 48% last year. Web companies such as Teladoc and American Well are expected to host some 1.2 million such virtual doctor visits this year, up 20% from last year, according to the American Telemedicine Association.

But critics worry that such services may be sacrificing quality for convenience. Consulting a random doctor patients will never meet, they say, further fragments the health-care system, and even minor issues such as upper respiratory(上呼吸道的) infections can't be thoroughly evaluated by a doctor who can't listen to your heart or feel your swollen glands. In a recent study, researchers posing as patients with skin problems sought help from 16 telemedicine sites—with unsettling results. In 62 encounters, fewer than one-third disclosed clinicians' credentials or let patients choose; only 32% discussed potential side effects of prescribed medications. Several sites misdiagnosed serious conditions, largely because they failed to ask basic follow-up questions, the researchers said. "Telemedicine holds enormous promise, but these sites are just not ready for prime time," says Jack Resneck, the study's lead author.

The American Telemedicine Association and other organizations have started accreditation(鉴定) programs to identify top-quality telemedicine sites. The American Medical Association this month approved new ethical guidelines for telemedicine, calling for participating doctors to recognize the limitations of such services and ensure that they have sufficient information to make clinical recommendations.

Who pays for the services? While employers and health plans have been eager to cover virtual urgent-care visits, insurers have been far less willing to pay for telemedicine when doctors use phone, email or video to consult with existing patients about continuing issues. "It's very hard to get paid unless you physically see the patient," says Peter Rasmussen, medical director of distance health at the Cleveland Clinic. Some 32 states have passed "parity"(等同的) laws requiring private insurers to reimburse doctors for services delivered remotely if the same service would be covered in person, though not necessarily at the same rate or frequency. Medicare lags further behind. The federal health plan for the elderly covers a small number of telemedicine services—only for beneficiaries in rural areas and only when the services are received in a hospital, doctor's office or clinic.

Bills to expand Medicare coverage of telemedicine have bipartisan(两党的) support in Congress. Opponents worry that such expansion would be costly for taxpayers, but advocates say it would save money in the long run.

Experts say more hospitals are likely to invest in telemedicine systems as they move away from fee-for- service payments and into managed-care-type contracts that give them a set fee to provide care for patients and allow them to keep any savings they achieve.

Is the state-by-state regulatory system outdated? Historically, regulation of medicine has been left to individual states. But some industry members contend that having 50 different sets of rules, licensing fees and even definitions of "medical practice" makes less sense in the era of telemedicine and is hampering its growth. Currently, doctors must have a valid license in the state where the patient is located to provide medical care, which means virtual-visit companies can match users only with locally licensed clinicians. It also causes administrative hassles(麻烦) for world-class medical centers that attract patients from across the country. At the Mayo Clinic, doctors who treat out-of-state patients can follow up with them via phone, email or web chats when they return home, but they can only discuss the conditions they treated in person. "If the patient wants to talk about a new problem, the doctor has to be licensed in that state to discuss it. If not, the patient should talk to his primary-care physician about it," says Steve Ommen, who runs Mayo's Connected Care program.

To date, 17 states have joined a compact that will allow a doctor licensed in one member state to quickly obtain a license in another. While welcoming the move, some telemedicine advocates would prefer states to automatically honor one another's licenses, as they do with drivers' licenses. But states aren't likely to surrender control of medical practice, and most are considering new regulations. This year, more than 200 telemedicine-related bills have been introduced in 42 states, many regarding what services Medicaid will cover and whether payers should reimburse for remote patient monitoring. "A lot of states are still trying to define telemedicine," says Lisa Robbin, chief advocacy officer for the Federation of State Medical Boards.

Many employers are eager to provide telemedicine service as a benefit to their employees because of its convenience.

careful.passage: Danielle Steel, the 71-year-old romance novelist is notoriously productive, having published 179 books at a rate of up to seven a year. But a passing reference in a recent profile by Glamour magazine to her 20-hour workdays prompted an outpouring of admiration. Steel has given that 20-hour figure when describing her "exhausting" process in the past: "I start the book and don't leave my desk until the first draft is finished." She goes from bed, to desk, to bath, to bed, avoiding all contact aside from phone calls with her nine children. "I don't comb my hair for weeks," she says. Meals are brought to her desk, where she types until her fingers swell and her nails bleed. The business news website Quartz held Steel up as an inspiration, writing that if only we all followed her "actually extremely liberating" example of industrious sleeplessness, we would be quick to see results. Well, indeed. With research results showing the cumulative effects of sleep loss and its impact on productivity, doubt has been voiced about the accuracy of Steel's self-assessment. Her output may be undeniable, but sceptics have suggested that she is guilty of erasing the role of ghost writers( 代笔人) at worst, gross exaggeration at best. Steel says working 20 hours a day is "pretty brutal physically." But is it even possible? "No," says Maryanne Taylor of the Sleep Works. While you could work that long, the impact on productivity would make it hardly worthwhile. If Steel was routinely sleeping for four hours a night, she would be drastically underestimating the negative impact, says Alison Gardiner, founder of the sleep improvement programme Sleep station. "It's akin to being drunk." It's possible that Steel is exaggerating the demands of her schedule. Self-imposed sleeplessness has "become a bit of a status symbol", says Taylor, a misguided measure to prove how powerful and productive you are. Margaret Thatcher was also said to get by on four hours a night, while the 130-hour workweeks endured by tech heads have been held up as key to their success. That is starting to change with increased awareness of the importance of sleep for mental health. "People are starting to realise that sleep should not be something that you fit in between everything else," says Taylor. But it is possible—if statistically extremely unlikely—that Steel could be born a "short sleeper" with an unusual body clock, says sleep expert Dr. Sophie Bostock. "It's probably present in fewer than 1% of the population." Even if Steel does happen to be among that tiny minority, says Bostock, it's "pretty irresponsible" to suggest that 20-hour days are simply a question of discipline for the rest of us.

careful.passage: Organic agriculture is a relatively untapped resource for feeding the Earth's population, especially in the face of climate change and other global challenges. That's the conclusion I reached in reviewing 40 years of science comparing the long-term prospects of organic and conventional farming. The review study, "Organic Agriculture in the 21st Century," is featured as the cover story for the February issue of the journal Nature Plants. It is the first to compare organic and conventional agriculture across the main goals of sustainability identified by the National Academy of Sciences: productivity, economics, and environment. Critics have long argued that organic agriculture is inefficient, requiring more land to yield the same amount of food. It's true that organic farming produces lower yields, averaging 10 to 20 percent less than conventional. Advocates contend that the environmental advantages of organic agriculture far outweigh the lower yields, and that increasing research and breeding resources for organic systems would reduce the yield gap. Sometimes excluded from these arguments is the fact that we already produce enough food to more than feed the world's 7.4 billion people but do not provide adequate access to all individuals. In some cases, organic yields can be higher than conventional. For example, in severe drought conditions, which are expected to increase with climate change in many areas, organic farms can produce as good, if not better, yields because of the higher water-holding capacity of organically farmed soils. What science does tell us is that mainstream conventional farming systems have provided growing supplies of food and other products but often at the expense of other sustainability goals. Conventional agriculture may produce more food, but it often comes at a cost to the environment. Biodiversity loss, environmental degradation, and severe impacts on ecosystem services have not only accompanied conventional farming systems but have often extended well beyond their field boundaries. With organic agriculture, environmental costs tend to be lower and the benefits greater. Overall, organic farms tend to store more soil carbon, have better soil quality, and reduce soil erosion compared to their conventional counterparts. Organic agriculture also creates less soil and water pollution and lower greenhouse gas emissions. And it's more energy-efficient because it doesn't rely on synthetic fertilizers or pesticides. Organic agriculture is also associated with greater biodiversity of plants, animals, insects and microorganisms as well as genetic diversity. Biodiversity increases the services that nature provides and improves the ability of farming systems to adapt to changing conditions. Despite lower yields, organic agriculture is more profitable for farmers because consumers are willing to pay more. Higher prices, called price premiums, can be justified as a way to compensate farmers for providing ecosystem services and avoiding environmental damage or external costs.

translation.source: 《红楼梦》(Dream of the Red Chamber )是18世纪曹雪芹创作的一部小说。曹雪芹基于自己痛苦的个人经 历,讲述了贾宝玉和林黛玉之间的悲剧性爱情故事。书中有大约30个主要人物和400多个次要人物,每个人物都刻 画得栩栩如生,具有鲜明的个性。小说详尽地描述了四个贵族世家兴衰的历程,反映了封建社会隐藏的种种危机 和错综复杂的社会冲突。 《红楼梦》融合了现实主义和浪漫主义,具有很强的艺术感染力。它被普遍认为是中 国最伟大的小说,也是世界上最伟大的文学创作之一。
translation.reference: Dream of the Red Chamber is a novel written by Cao Xueqin in the 18th century. Based on his own painful personal experience, Cao Xueqin told the tragic love story between Jia Baoyu and Lin Daiyu. There are about 30 major characters and more than 400 minor ones in the book, and each character is portrayed vividly, with a distinct personality. The novel describes in detail the rise and fall of four aristocratic families, and reflects the hidden crises and complicated social conflicts of feudal society. It combines realism and romanticism, and has great artistic appeal. It is widely regarded as the greatest novel in China and one of the greatest literary works in the world.
